20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><strong>Transcript</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s kind of hard to believe, but the original Borat movie was 20 years ago. It’s time for a second sequel. And I already have the title. It would be Corruption for Make Benefit Glorious Family of Trump. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I hope that some of my listeners are young enough to not remember the original Borat movie. But it was a mockumentary, a satire, in which Sacha Baron Cohen pretended to be a journalist from Kazakhstan investigating and interviewing Americans about American mores. It was not about Kazakhstan, although he did insult the country along the way. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The reason I think about it is that today’s New York Times has a piece that reports, investigative reporting, on an immense mining deal in Kazakhstan, which, what do you know, turns out to be a big profit center for the Trump sons and also the sons of Howard Lutnick, the Commerce Secretary. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Check out the investigative reporting for the details, but basically here’s another one, another big one.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s part of an immense series of corrupt deals, often with petrostates — which Kazakhstan is — that financially benefit Donald Trump and his family and some of his cronies and cabinet members as well and their families. It’s all on a truly epic scale. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is a message I have been trying to get across. I don’t think many people even now understand just how much of a departure what’s happening now is from past US history. I still see people saying we might be, could be heading for another Gilded Age. But we have a level of concentration of wealth in the hands of a few people that is something like three times what it was at the peak of the Gilded Age. We’re in a super duper Gilded Age. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And I sometimes hear people say, well, could we be returning to old kinds of corruption? Might we have another Teapot Dome scandal? Well, my God. Teapot Dome was a scandal actually involving mineral rights and bribes during the Harding administration, although not bribes to the president’s family, which is, again, something entirely new. The scale of the bribes was about $500,000: adjusting for inflation, that’s something like $9 million today.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So how much has Trump enriched himself since returning to the White House about 500 days ago? The answer is certainly more than four billion dollars, almost certainly more than four and a half, maybe five billion dollars. Divide that by 500 and we basically have a Teapot Dome sized corruption scandal on an average day under Trump.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So it’s basically day after day of scandals as big or bigger than Teapot Dome. Our corrupt grandfathers, great-grandfathers were pikers compared with this, just as the Gilded Age robber barons were pikers compared with the modern-day tech bros. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is obviously not good. It’s actually quite horrifying. How did we so quickly descend into becoming a truly massively corrupt country on a level that we used to think of as being associated only with tinpot dictators in the third world? And yet here we are. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This ought to be a political issue and it ought to be a legal issue as soon as the government is back in the hands of people who actually take the rule of law seriously. Again, without going into the details of the deal, it’s surely illegal. I mean, it’s illegal under the Emoluments Clause. Probably since there are definitely Kazakhs on the take as well, it’s illegal under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. This is just, it’s illegal up the wazoo.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Of course, it will not be prosecuted as long as Trump is in the White House. But forget any Democrat who isn’t promising to go after this massive corruption when they regain power. If they don’t, then none of this matters, but that should be a core part of anybody’s platform. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I’m not a political expert — sometimes I think nobody is — but my God, again, this corruption is so blatant. And it does resonate with people. It’s really clear that corruption at the top and the sense that ordinary people are paying the price while people with power enrich themselves is an effective popular issue. That is actually the issue that brought Viktor Orban down in Hungary, which is one of the hopeful signs for what may happen to America going down the pike. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So here we are, just to remind you that this scandal, it’s a huge thing. It’s page one in the New York Times, but in a way it’s actually kind of ordinary, since even this size of scandal is happening every few weeks these days.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Do not make the mistake of treating what’s going on as in any sense normal. This is hugely abnormal, and I believe that the American people will understand that it’s abnormal even if pundits get bored of talking about the corruption. So drive it home, maybe for make benefit American people instead of the Trump family.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. Santiago</a><span> via Getty Images)</span></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I don’t want to exacerbate the tendency for everything that happens in New York to attract more attention than it deserves by writing a post specifically pooh-poohing the Democratic Socialists of America’s big primary wins there. What I do want to say is that part of what makes the wins such an impressive organizational flex is that the people they beat are themselves very left-wing. Even on Israel, it’s not like any of the losers were big pro-Israel outliers. Ritchie Torres, the actual noteworthy moderate among the New York City delegation, won his primary easily. So I don’t know what the stakes are here. I think people will discover that replacing House members who are to the left of the median Democrat with members who are somewhat further left doesn’t actually change anything — and I would caution moderates against getting too emotionally invested in this kind of race. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another thing that happened this week is that the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3f421d7a-c198-44d6-9090-ee9d47cd352c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Adam Gray/Tom Suozzi Promise to America movement</a><span> signed up eight new members of Congress. They include Vicente Gonzalez, Don Davis, and Laura Gillen, who are holding down some of the caucus’s toughest seats, along with Kristen McDonald Rivet, an electoral superstar who should have been the establishment’s choice for the Michigan Senate race. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>They also picked up some congressional </span><em>candidates</em><span> including Bobby Pulido, who is going to be a huge star if he manages to win a tough race in a gerrymandered seat in South Texas, and Jamie Ager, a farmer running in North Carolina who is actually practicing a kind of throwback rural politics rather than just marketing that kind of politics to college graduates. I saw some </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cc43c116-01cf-48ab-a98f-0efb8bed2576?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">speculation on Twitter</a><span> about why the leftist insurgency isn’t gaining ground in Chicago, but the obvious answer is the left </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c1b4f00c-0175-47a0-bfb9-6d20fe58c25a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">already won power in Chicago and voters have hated it</a><span>, so the left doesn’t talk about Chicago anymore. In the Bay Area, Matt Mahan and Dan Lurie are leading a wave of pro-growth reformist mayors who represent what comes after left-wing failures, and I think we’ll see a movement like that emerge in Chicago too. That doesn’t mean failure is inevitable — you can always pursue the Zohran Mamdani path of keeping his predecessor’s key policies on crime and education in place, not raising taxes on city residents or city businesses, and focusing on zoning reform and foreign policy. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But it’s just to say that the real work is not fighting rear-guard actions on behalf of lifelong progressives who’ve just fallen out of step with the fashions of the time. It’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e36a86c0-2fd7-40d6-9b8e-aa05d38d61e8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">building the next thing</a><span>.</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-a03?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=280280464" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Amos Karlsen:</span></a><span> A couple of (maybe) contradictions about public opinion I’ve been wondering about lately: (1) People are loathe to acknowledge tradeoffs, eg wanting to cut taxes but not spending, yet also excessively zero-sum, eg thinking Trump must be solid on economics to balance out his poor character/corruption/election stealing attempts. (2) Everyone is super negative/pessimistic about politics, and yet also seem to believe unrealistic promises like Biden unifying the country or Trump lowering prices — or at least believe them enough to be disappointed when they don’t come to fruition. Not sure if there’s an explanation here, or if I’m just mischaracterizing the situation, but feels like maybe something weird going on.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These are shrewd observations on your part, and I think it’s largely all </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/55ae3711-3267-4732-b201-73a49b6d283d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>downstream of the stealth democracy phenomenon</span></a><span> that gives rise to these populist paradoxes. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’ve written about this before, but, to briefly recap, the thesis of the book by Elizabeth Theiss-Morse and John R. Hibbing is that most of the public is fundamentally hostile to what political scientists would consider the normal operation of a democratic republic. That is to say, voters view the existence of sharp partisan conflict as evidence that key actors in the system are not on the level. If people of goodwill and integrity sit down around the table, they should be able to just work things out and solve problems. This is not true. But if you keep in mind that most people </span><em><span>think</span></em><span> that it’s true, a lot of other phenomena snap into place. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Notably, this reconciles the aversion to acknowledging tradeoffs with the tendency toward an excessively zero-sum worldview. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A tradeoff-acknowledger says that generous pensions and medical care for the elderly sound good because the elderly are broadly sympathetic, but also that dedicating large amounts of resources to this is bad for economic growth. One reason that political conflict exists among people of goodwill and integrity is that wanting to take care of the elderly and wanting to ensure economic growth are both totally reasonable ideas, but there is a conflict, so reasonable people disagree about what to do. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the stealth democracy framework rejects that. It can’t possibly be the case that democratic disagreement exists among people of goodwill due to genuine tradeoffs. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What </span><em><span>can</span></em><span> be the case is that corrupt or malign forces are appropriating resources to clearly illegitimate ends. So we get people adopting a very zero-sum view of immigrants or billionaires or believing that if we eliminate USAID or stop giving money to Israel that somehow all these tradeoffs will vanish. </span></p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>By the same token, excessive negativism about the people currently holding political office lends itself to excessive optimism about the scope for change if we elect someone new. On the prices, for example, it’s not just that actually lowering the price level is probably impossible. The reality is that the Biden administration spent a lot of time thinking about ideas to reduce inflation and interest rates. What they kept bumping up against is that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/872f70c6-7b03-4c55-a459-cf997511e2be?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>the main way to accomplish this is deficit reduction</span></a><span>. I think that all things considered, they should have gone for it. But the counter-argument that all the feasible roads to deficit reduction are somewhat politically unpalatable isn’t crazy. The problem is that voters look at an inflation situation they think is bad and assume the bad situation is happening because bad people are running the government. If you just got some good people in there, they would fix things. So then Trump comes in and he’s just dealing with the same basic situation and for broadly similar reasons he doesn’t fix things. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now there’s a lot of people on the left who feel that if they just overthrow “the Democratic establishment” and put one of their own into the White House, it will both slay MAGA and also solve all the fundamental problems of American life. That’s exactly how a lot of people felt 20 years ago, and it powered Barack Obama’s presidential campaign and took him all the way to the White House. I think Obama was a good president — maybe even a great one — but the people who projected the most unrealistic hopes onto him ended up sharply disappointed and today insist that he “betrayed” them on behalf of the corrupt establishment he was supposed to overthrow. What mostly happened is that he had to wrestle with reality. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My sense is that a lot of what plays to ideologues these days as hard-left politics is actually just a further manifestation of stealth democracy. You could imagine a world in which the rising clout of the left meant that more and more people were calling for a 25 percent VAT or for higher income taxes on </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/daf2f902-71fb-470f-95ec-df7fd716b15c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>the whole top half of the income distribution</span></a><span>.  </span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are real merits to this way of doing things, but it involves a fairly explicit tradeoff — in the Nordic countries, lots of banal consumer goods are less affordable than in the United States, but social goods like health care and child care and education are cheaper. But that kind of ethic of solidarity is absolutely </span><em>not</em><span> what the insurgent left is promoting. What they’re saying is that if we get rid of the corrupt politicians who are in the pockets of billionaires, we can just all get this stuff for free and not give anything up. This is just not really true, and it’s quite different from the practice of actually existing social democracies. But it’s appealing for the same reason that MAGA Twitter is always insisting to me that we can solve all housing problems and also balance the budget by deporting illegal immigrants. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-a03?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=280825365" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Robert Bonasia:</span></a></strong><span> </span><strong><span>Is there a clear path for an urban Democrat to contend in swing states or nationally or are the primary electorates that choose them too left wing?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>In Philadelphia the mayor is regularly labeled a “centrist,” but this mostly means she thinks heroin users should go to rehab instead of being allowed to shoot up on the street. She also signed sanctuary city legislation and heavy handed tenant protections into law without pushback. Keisha Lance Bottoms has a shot in Georgia, but that seems downstream of national political trends. In the past Ed Rendell went from being mayor of Philadelphia to governor of Pennsylvania, despite running in a strong midterm for Republicans. Is the only path now to be a Mamdani type, run for President and pray you get a nominated in a blue wave?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is obviously a tough one. To get elected mayor of Philadelphia, you need to appeal to the median Democratic Party primary voter in the city of Philadelphia and you need to do so without relying on electability arguments. To get elected governor of Pennsylvania, you need to appeal to true swing voters. There’s just a big gap there. As you say, these kinds of cities routinely do elect moderate mayors relative to the local factional politics, but someone like that is probably still extremely progressive. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But I don’t think this is an ironclad law of politics. Mike Duggan served 12 years as a popular and successful mayor of Detroit, and I think he could have been a successful statewide politician. He decided he wanted to run for governor and also decided that he was actually too moderate to win a Democratic primary, so he was going to try to run as an independent. That didn’t work and he’s dropped out. But I think that was clearly poor decision-making on his part. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The key thing about Duggan, in contrast to Cherelle </span><span>Parker in Philadelphia or my outgoing mayor in D.C., is that his political profile was as a successful reformer rather than as a “custodian of the establishment who fended off the leftists.” </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Presumably at some point, the left faction will win a mayor’s race in Philadelphia. And then after some number of years in power they will stumble and lose control to a moderate. That person will then come in and do some moderate reformist stuff in a way that generates a very different statewide and national profile from the establishment custodian profile. Dan Lurie in San Francisco, for example, is clearly the kind of person who could do well in a swing state. His problem is that California isn’t a swing state, so it’s not clear that having a profile that’s mostly about being a moderate reformer is good for him. But Lurie is a guy who has plenty of progressive positions on the issues — it’s </span><em>San Francisco</em><span> — the difference is that he leads a newish moderate political regime that took over and enacted a bunch of noteworthy moderate changes. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-a03?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=280398280" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Andrew:</a><span> Why is it hard to get focused on results in politics? Like this is a big thread in abundance and once you start looking for it it’s everywhere.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>We have checks we send out but actually doing the things isn’t nearly as important.</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A fundamental reality of American politics is that the vast majority of elected officials are backbench legislators in safe seats who are looking for promotion to a better job. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Conditional on being a backbench legislator in a safe seat, there is really only one way to deliver “results” and it’s to do what Elizabeth Warren and Tim Scott did with the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act: Find a partner across the aisle, roll up your sleeves, and do some stuff. You can be a moderate who crafts bipartisan deals or you can be a progressive icon who crafts bipartisan deals, but bipartisan deals are how things get done. It’s not that all legislation is bipartisan, but a lot of it is. And the partisan bills that pass are very leadership-driven processes with a lot of input from the White House. As a normal member of Congress, bipartisan dealmaking is the way to get things done. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’d love to live in a world where Chris Murphy’s work on the bipartisan asylum reform bill that Trump killed in 2024 was a big boost to his presidential ambitions and his vague musings about the evils of neoliberalism were a hindrance. Realistically, though, it’s the opposite. The best thing Murphy has done to advance his </span><em>career</em><span> is hazy takes, and if he ever becomes a serious contender, his bipartisan legislative work is likely to become a vulnerability. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For Warren and the ROAD to Housing Act, there’s no real downside risk because the person who would attack a Democrat for doing this bill is Warren herself. Because she is literally Elizabeth Warren, nobody is going to complain that she sold out to banking interests and private equity. But there’s still no real tangible upside for her. She gets to know that she accomplished something on an important issue and I hope that’s reward enough for her. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But for the majority of politicians — especially House members and the thousands of largely anonymous state legislators and local legislative officeholders — the name of the game is to make all your party’s interest group stakeholders like you. That’s the way to build a case for yourself as you try to move up the ladder. And that’s antithetical to the spirit of getting things done. It’s true that the handful of members in swing seats have </span><em>more</em><span> incentive to get deals done. But the easiest way to be a moderate is just to say “no” to all of your party’s controversial ideas — to do less, not more. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So you’re left with a relatively tiny number of executive officeholders as the only real constituency for results. The governor wants to open the bridge. The mayor wants to tout falling crime. </span><em>They</em><span> need to care about results. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But the public is not always very good at causal attribution. One of the biggest differences between Zohran Mamdani’s successful run as a progressive mayor and Brandon Johnson’s failed run as a progressive mayor is that Johnson had to deal with the fallout of the Biden-era asylum situation and Mamdani didn’t. But it’s still the case that in terms of what you can actually control, an executive’s best bet is to try to deliver good results. </p><p class="button-wrapper" href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-a03?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=280530418" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>JohnFromNewHampshire:</span></a><span> We’ve been powering aircraft carriers and submarines with nuclear reactors for decades. Seems like a huge environmental and economic win to let cargo fleets use the technology. Is there any hope for this?</span><span> </span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Back during the Biden administration, there was a diplomatic agreement between the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia under which the Australian Navy would </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9ae02a6e-4863-4ecc-ae51-b7924fe7ccfb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">buy some nuclear-powered submarines</a><span>, so we got to witness an English-language debate about the value of this technology. What I learned is that separate from the national security issues around exporting military-grade nuclear reactors, there’s just a significant cost premium for nuclear propulsion over diesel. Countries like South Korea and Japan that almost certainly could either develop domestic reactor designs or else do an Australia-style deal to buy them have chosen to do neither of those things. The thinking is that given the budget constraint, it is better to have a larger number of diesel subs rather than a smaller number of nuclear ones. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The case </span><em>for</em><span> nuclear in a naval context is that nuclear propulsion has desirable performance characteristics — notably, it can run for years without needing to refuel — that are worth paying a premium for. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the specific context of ballistic missile submarines used for strategic deterrence, this is extremely valuable and that’s why the U.S., the U.K., and France all have them. It is also why the People’s Republic of China built the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b0218f6f-fb06-47af-8c8e-5e9afe830ec9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Type 094 submarine</a><span> and is developing its successor, the Type 096. So the ballistic missile subs are a clear case for nuclear propulsion. There’s then a decent case that if you want to build a fleet of attack subs to hunt and potentially destroy enemy ballistic missile subs, you need nuclear propulsion for that mission, too. But it’s debatable. The core use case really is nuclear deterrence. So even though the “carry nuclear warheads” and “use a nuclear reactor for power” aspects of a nuclear submarine fleet are conceptually separate, in practice they tend to go together. Australia is breaking that pattern, but it’s a borderline call. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The upshot is that there’s no reason to think civilian cargo ships would </span><em>want</em><span> to use naval reactor technology. The U.S. itself experimented with nuclear-powered cruisers and destroyers only to abandon the idea as not meeting a cost-benefit test. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For cargo, the case looks even worse. It would be cool, I suppose, to have a container ship that didn’t need to refuel. But the whole point of a container ship is to make regular stops at ports to load and unload. So there’s nothing really here that civilian shipbuilders would want. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It seems to me that the real relevance the nuclear-powered navy offers to civilian energy issues comes from another angle. These naval reactors are not subject to Nuclear Regulatory Commission oversight or any of its procedures for licensing reactor designs. And yet, the safety track record of the nuclear-powered navy is excellent. Which doesn’t mean we should just start rolling out naval reactors for civilian purposes — for starters, these reactors are designed to produce a lot of direct propulsion rather than electricity, so it wouldn’t even work — but it does go to show that a regulatory framework oriented around “getting to yes” on reactor designs can be perfectly safe and we don’t need the precautionary principle ethos that’s dominated the N.R.C. since its inception. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-a03?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=280427782" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">A New Jerusalem:</a><span> </span><span>I know we’ve been worried about the Road to Housing Act crippling the build to rent market. I sort of don’t understand why the build to rent market exists when the cost to buy versus rent is so high in most cities. Is this an artifact of some zoning distortion? That most of the current buy versus rent cost is from interest rates so developers aren’t pocketing the benefit?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Build-to-rent single-family housing exists because:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Most residentially zoned land prohibits multi-family development. </p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Since 2008, we’ve made it harder to get a mortgage. </p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>(2) means lots of people need to rent and (1) means that even though we are building more apartments post-2008 than we were pre-2008, you can’t fully accommodate the demand through that channel. ROAD ultimately resolved in a happy place where build-to-rent is protected, and it also includes provisions that should help generate relief on both (1) and (2). I’m less bullish </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3d2ac334-389a-4f65-b049-c25fbff31b85?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">than Kevin Erdmann</a><span> on the wisdom of going all the way back on (2) to where we were previously, but I do think everyone needs to recognize that there was an overcorrection there. Ultimately, though, the point is that people need to live somewhere. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you want them to live in owner-occupied housing, you need to give them mortgages. If you want them to rent, then you need to legalize rental projects. Traditionally that has meant apartments, and nobody is more in favor of legalizing apartments than I am. But even in YIMBYtopia there’s lots of cheap land in America (in fact, in YIMBYtopia a lot of the land would get cheaper) and it makes more sense to develop that as detached homes. Why shouldn’t some of that inventory be rentals?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-a03?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=280292496" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Chris:</a><span> You’re mayor of New York. A developer comes to you with a plan: eminent domain a whole block of brownstones in, let’s say East Village, raze it, and replace it with a tower(s)-on-a-base development. You’d replace ~500 housing units with 3,000. You’d add retail space and enough underground parking to remove some nearby on-street parking. But you’d completely change the NYC aesthetic of the neighborhood. Do you do it?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>No, of course not, and I think the specter of using eminent domain powers in this context reflects how far off the mark the basic politics of housing have become in the U.S. Nobody should force existing landowners to raze their properties or sell out to new developers. The incredibly radical change that we need to make to residential land use in the U.S. is to </span><em>allow people to voluntarily sell their property to developers if they want to</em><span>. On 90 percent of parcels in 90 percent of locations, the upshot of making that change will be — nothing. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Most people who own homes don’t particularly want to sell them. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And in most cases, the economics of demolishing a perfectly good home in order to build a different structure on the same location aren’t very appealing. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But it is also the case that there are some parcels of land that are currently so undersupplied with housing that a developer would be willing to make a really strong bid for a teardown prospect. And in any given year, some of the people who own parcels of land like that develop a strong motive to move to another location or to realize the financial gains of their housing investment. So you could go from a situation where there are no teardown re-developments in a given neighborhood to a situation where a few happen in any given year. Scale that across a lot of different neighborhoods in a lot of metro areas across a large country and you get a lot of additional housing. Scale it temporally for a long span of time, and you get a country where the built environment of neighborhoods changes faster but the sociological processes of displacement actually happen slower. You have more jobs, more tax revenue, faster economic growth, higher productivity, and so forth. But there’s no case for seizing people’s land in low-density areas and forcibly redeveloping it at higher density. There would be massive backlash to that and you’d eliminate the best arguments for YIMBYism. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Note that you picked out a specific case where I think almost anyone will agree that the forced re-development would be economically beneficial. But adopting that as a systematic approach would just </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6627d97c-8376-45c4-8ce2-f409683168f2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">recapitulate all the sins of urban planning as a genre</a><span> — by ignoring market forces, you’d inevitably end up missing the mark on what the real “correct” scale of development is. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The critical thing that we need to do is to acknowledge that real estate markets feature a very complicated set of tradeoffs. Any individual non-billionaire is going to end up making some kind of compromise. Either you spend a larger share of your income on housing than is desirable, or you get a smaller place than is optimal, or you end up in a location that falls short of ideal in terms of commute logistics or some aspect of local amenities or whatever else. Markets let people work out not just “what would I like” but how much do I like X versus Y and how much I am willing to give up to get it. We should let neighborhoods evolve and change in response to shifts in demand, but not force them to change. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-a03?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=280598125" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Thomas L. Hutcheson:</span></a><span> What do, should Democrats DO if they win House and Senate?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What they should do is investigate Trump scandals while advancing a limited economic agenda of popular measures — a modest minimum-wage hike and a restoration of the health care funding that was cut under Trump — along with political reforms like bans on congressional stock trading and gerrymandering. But looking at how House primaries have gone, what they probably </span><em><span>will</span></em><span> do is immediately lapse into factional infighting about Israel. </span></p><p Econ</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Solopreneurship has been increasing since 2008, both in absolute terms and as a percent of new business formation. Some of this is due to legal changes. The Obamacare exchanges make it easier for solopreneurs to buy their own health insurance. The Qualified Business Income deduction, the simplified home-office deduction, and other tax changes have made it more favorable to be a solopreneur. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">On top of that, the internet made a lot of solo business models easier to execute, from dropshipping businesses to YouTube channels to subscription-based email newsletters. I am a solopreneur myself — Noahpinion is an S-corporation. Substack made it incredibly easy for me to sell and deliver content online, Twitter/X made it incredibly easy for me to market that content, and Stripe made it incredibly easy to receive payments — all without hiring anyone. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The team at Stripe Economics argues that this latter trend is just getting started. Thanks to AI, the number of business models that can be executed by single individuals is growing rapidly:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An agent can now help you find the best tools for your business and handle your integration with minimal support….The recent growth in nonemployer businesses shows a positive relationship with industry-level AI adoption…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Part of the reason businesses historically tended to be built by groups was that a single individual rarely possesses all the skills needed in the entrepreneurial journey. Whether it’s how to evaluate or size a market, code an app, price a product, write and execute a marketing campaign, or close a deal, AI (and AI-augmented software) can fill many of the gaps that founders previously turned to another human for. Or, as Sam Altman so succinctly put it: “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/07debfda-ec8c-4abb-937f-408c639b153d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"><span>revenge of the idea guys</span></a><span>.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We think this phenomenon is the true engine of the AI surge in business formation we’re seeing today. The availability of this breadth of on-tap assistance allows anyone with sufficient motivation to go it alone. Given this, we think the 20% figure is a floor rather than a ceiling in terms of AI impact.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This makes sense. It’s pretty clear that one big reason to have a multi-person company has always been </span><em>individual specialization</em><span>. But Claude is far more versatile than any human being, so in the age of AI agents, specialization will probably be less important in many cases. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Even in the (many) cases where that doesn’t allow one person to run a company all by themself, it will tend to push companies toward lower headcount. Kim and Koning have </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/34afd8ea-8c01-4aef-9e24-55e97bd40204?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a new working paper</a><span> showing that “AI-native” companies now being created tend to have about 25% fewer employees than their peers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is important, because it bears on the future of human employment — the question that’s currently on almost everyone’s minds. It raises the possibility that </span><em>self-employment is the future of employment</em><span>. It’s easy enough to imagine a future in which relying on a group of other humans for your economic sustenance won’t be as important — instead, we’ll all be like little private ship captains, ordering around our crews of AI agents. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That future is easy to envision because it’s the logical endpoint of a trend that had already been going on for quite some time: the rise of corporate outsourcing. Whether it was manufacturing supply chains </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/93cf63c0-9ab2-4da1-9921-f28cddadcad6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">strung out across dozens of countries</a><span>, or companies hiring subcontractors to do their payroll or their IT or their accounting, or corporations paying SaaS providers for software products, companies generally </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9b0998cd-4c4e-4a40-a7ed-6a5eb1fd5aee?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">do a lot less of their work in-house</a><span> than they did half a century ago. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The rise of outsourcing — both domestic and foreign — was enabled by improvements in transportation and communication technologies. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1ee1fcb5-fbf8-4273-8bab-0d4953ea1e65?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Shipping crates</a><span> and the internet made it easy to turn local production networks into regional or global ones. The internet made it easy to find contractors, verify their reputability, communicate with them, and monitor them to verify their work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That fit very well with the leading economics theory of outsourcing: </span><strong>transaction cost theory</strong><span>. First advanced </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fbe4c9a6-cc00-47a4-b55f-f2918c9a051b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">by Ronald Coase in the 1930s</a><span> and later refined </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/57605d4a-0a85-4049-b78b-4f2fdff75682?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">by Oliver Williamson</a><span> and others, transaction cost theory says that companies exist because it’s sometimes cheaper and easier to execute transactions in-house than at arm’s length. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Consider the process of paying the workers at a factory. In 1937, for a company to get some other company to handle their payroll would have been a very arduous process. You would have had to look up payroll contractors in the phone book, ask around to find out whether each one had a good reputation, have their representatives come by your factory to get information about how many hours each worker had worked, and so on. Far easier to just walk down the hall to your own payroll division and have them do it. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But by 2007, this calculus had switched — thanks to the internet, it was fairly easy to do all that stuff at arm’s length, online. This allowed specialization at the level of the firm rather than at the level of the division or the employee — in other words, corporate outsourcing.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That’s just a story, of course. But in general, transaction cost theory is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/533823c3-75be-467e-8a88-952e58a77125?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">strongly supported</a><span> by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ef6cd0b2-5877-4ede-9620-ac73d6cb3bb5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">empirical evidence</a><span>; in cases where we can measure transaction costs, they do seem to affect the decision to in-house versus outsource. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/09857fb7-4e92-4928-bc63-50642d5db93b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Bergeaud et al. (2023)</a><span> find evidence that the internet drove a wave of outsourcing in France, for example:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Does domestic outsourcing react to technological change? We study the staggered diffusion of broadband internet in France in the 2000s, and show that connected firms increased their outsourcing expenditures while decreasing the diversity of occupations they employ in-house…Overall, we show that the deployment of new technologies stimulated domestic outsourcing in this context[.]</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There are other theories about why companies choose to do things themselves versus buying them from someone else, but many of them — incomplete contracts theory, agency theory, relational contracting theory, etc. — overlap substantially with transaction cost theory. The informality, close monitoring, and long-term relationships that form within a company can all be seen as ways of decreasing transaction costs.  </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A lot of people are assuming that when it comes to transaction costs, AI will work like the internet, only more so. (In fact, I find “AI will be like the internet, only more so” to be one of the most common tacit assumptions in AI discourse in general.) AI can read, understand, and analyze your business’s website in an instant — or dispense with the need of a website entirely. It can scan the entire internet to assess whether your business is a trustworthy contractor, or even contact you directly to find out. It can absorb nearly unlimited reams of business data, in order to monitor that you’re doing a good job. And so on.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s easy to see how this might lead to a world of total outsourcing and solopreneurs. But at the same time, it’s possible to imagine that AI will </span><em>increase</em><span> transaction costs between companies. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The simple reason is that AI doesn’t just analyze information; it also creates it. Yes, an AI can search the web for payroll outsourcing companies and get an idea of which are reputable by researching everything that has ever been said about each. But by the same token, an AI can create a new company, give it a website, and invent a bunch of other companies and reviewers to make it look legit. And then if and when your AI pays that AI’s fake company to do your accounting or whatever, the fake company can just take all your money and vanish in a puff of smoke.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI-driven fraud is already happening, at scale. Here’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5e401d51-9dc4-44ce-aea7-f5003b6f7108?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a BBC story from last year</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Unscrupulous foreign firms are using AI-generated images and false back stories to pose as family-run UK businesses to lure in shoppers…Customers say they feel “completely ripped off”…Consumer guide </span><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aff56e79-0134-46a0-b04f-003744482976?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Which?</a></strong><span> said the growing use of AI tools was making it possible for fraudsters to mislead the public on an “unprecedented” scale.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If human consumers can be fooled, so can human purchasing agents and procurement specialists. “OK,” you respond, “I’ll just get an AI to do the purchasing and procurement. Problem solved.” </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But here we are, back in the realm of </span><em>transaction costs</em><span>. You might need a frontier AI and a lot of expensive tokens to check the ever-expanding galaxy of fake companies in a way that would allow you to make a reliable outsourcing decision. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Nor would it even necessarily take fraud and manipulation in order to make arm’s-length transactions between AIs unreliable. Human beings are relatively consistent over time — if I do business with you today, I can be reasonably sure that doing business with you tomorrow will be similar, because your knowledge and skills and character etc. are all going to be roughly the same. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is </span><em>not</em><span> generally true with AI — at least, not with the AIs that exist today. They are ephemeral creatures; their ability to maintain the same goals, personalities, and capabilities over the weeks or months or even years of a business-to-business contractor relationship has yet to be demonstrated. So in the world where everyone doing business is an AI agent, even if your company verifies that it’s dealing with a real and honest contractor, that verification might not hold for long. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If AIs remain inconsistent over time, trust will therefore have to be reestablished from scratch every so often, and that could be expensive. In fact, we’ve already seen an example of just how expensive constant re-verification of trust can be: </span><em>Bitcoin</em><span>. In order to do away with the need for intermediaries like banks to verify transactions, Bitcoin has to reestablish trust between counterparties </span><em>every time a transaction is performed</em><span>. As </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2b646c4c-42ae-4dfe-a223-b69b470e13e1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Eric Budish has shown</a><span>, constant reestablishment of trust is incredibly expensive in terms of electricity, which basically dooms Bitcoin’s use as a medium of exchange.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So AI doesn’t have to be an unreliable partner in order to put an end to the world of ubiquitous online contracting that we’ve built over the past three decades. All it has to be is </span><em>a partner whose reliability is expensive to verify</em><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If AI brings about a world of </span><em>higher</em><span> transaction costs, due to the inherent unreliability of long-term arm’s-length dealings between AI agents, then the AI age will probably be one of </span><em>bigger</em><span> companies. Internal procedures for verifying trustworthiness — the AI equivalent of walking down the hall and knocking on the door of your own internal corporate division — might be the new equivalent of the informal long-term relationships that lower transaction costs within a typical human-staffed company. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0b8ae26c-c5da-4ed6-a9ef-d99dc2578d3a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a post back in April</a><span>, I predicted that Japan-style “salarymen” occupations — ever-shifting irregular bundles of tasks within a single big company — might be a more important kind of job all around the world going forward. But the transaction cost theory of the firm could give us another reason to expect the same. If only big companies can establish internal trust cheaply, then many humans — whatever kind of work they’re still doing 10 or 30 years from now — will be working for big companies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That doesn’t mean solopreneurship is a temporary trend or a dead end. There are probably many lines of business in which long-term trust between agents carrying out specialized business processes is not a big deal. In those areas, solopreneurs will flourish. We may thus see a bifurcated distribution of company sizes and job types — a vast horde of solopreneurs, and a few monster companies employing huge numbers of wage earners. </p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><div class="subscribe-widget is-signed-up is-fully-subscribed" stunning failure in Iran has weakened </span><span>America </span><span>on many fronts. </span><span>The world now perceives us as </span><span>neither a reliable ally nor an invincible enemy</span><span>, with an extortionately expensive military that is losing its best and brightest to Pete Hegseth’s prejudice and incompetence. We are now four months into a war that was supposed to last a couple of weeks.There is no end in sight as strikes and counter-strikes continue despite Trump’s farcical proclamations of American victory and Iranian surrender. Sixteen months into his presidency, Trump has squandered all of America’s credibility with the rest of the world.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So let me add one more item to the </span><span>tally of destruction:</span><span> The supremacy of the dollar</span><span>, the pre-eminent tool in America’s toolbox of global financial power,</span><span> has been seriously damaged</span><span> by the rise of alternative payment systems – a rise that was greatly hastened by the Iran war.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let me be clear that I </span><em>don’t</em><span> mean that the dollar is </span><span>close to losing </span><span>its dominant role in global business. And I am definitely not claiming that </span><span>the dollar’s weakened status </span><span>will make the United States </span><span>substantially </span><span>poorer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Instead, what I am talking about </span><span>is the loss of a </span><span>non-military</span><span> tool of coercion — the</span><span> </span><span>power to punish that </span><span>the dominant role of the dollar in international financial transactions </span><span>gave the United States. That power is now greatly diminished because </span><span>Trump’s Iran </span><span>war demonstrated </span><span>to other nations that they can</span><span> bypass the dollar-centered world payments system</span><span> — largely thanks to China</span><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Let me </span><span>provide context </span><span>by talking about the dollar’s global role.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The </span><span>dollar’s importance in international financial transactions far outweighs the U.S. economy’s global importance. America </span><span>is by no means a dominant force in world trade or world GDP. There are, in fact, three roughly comparable-sized economic superpowers in today’s world: China, the United States, and the European Union. However, the U.S. dollar does play a dominant role in world finance. There are multiple aspects to this role, which I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8701aec4-16af-44c7-a4a9-39ffadbba3da?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">discussed at length</a><span> in April. But one number make</span><span>s</span><span> the point: Last year </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d1587ba7-323b-415e-a7c8-99fc0b15978b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">89 percent</a><span> of foreign exchange transactions — transactions in which one nation’s currency is exchanged for another — involved U.S. dollars.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>How is this possible, when the U.S. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e34a7472-4a65-4690-a2f4-307581df7690?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">share of world exports</a><span> is only around 10 percent? The answer is that the dollar is the world’s “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dcc88d28-8ab1-4b9a-9f3f-4a06dcd7af7b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">vehicle currency</a><span>” — the currency businesses use to make transits between other currencies. A bank that wants to exchange, say, Indian rupees for British pounds generally won’t try to find a counterparty who wants to make the reverse trade. It will, instead, sell rupees for dollars and then use the dollars to buy pounds.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why does everyone use dollars? Because so many other people and businesses use dollars, which makes markets in dollars far more liquid and efficient than markets in any other currency. As a classic old paper by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9b24cc18-6304-4f48-82e6-c0881ee03070?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Charles Kindleberger</a><span> pointed out, the dollar’s role as a global currency is similar to the role of English as a global business language: Everyone speaks English because everyone else does. When people warn that the dollar is at imminent risk of losing its status to, say, the Chinese yuan, my response is to ask how long they think it will be before businesspeople around the world begin making deals in Mandarin.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Furthermore, the economic advantage to the U.S. of owning the premier global currency — our “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b18245a9-2c14-4224-96a7-b9f698906672?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">exorbitant privilege</a><span>,” a term coined by </span><span>Valéry Giscard d’Estaing in the 1960s — is not, despite what one sometimes hears, essential to U.S. prosperity. Our overall economic strength rests not on the role of the dollar but on our productivity and our leadership in science and technology. (The Trump administration is doing its best to destroy the latter, but that’s another story.)</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What dollar dominance does do, however, is give America a powerful economic weapon against other nations. Transactions that involve dollar payments normally require transferring money between U.S. banks — which means that they are visible to and can be blocked by U.S. authorities. In the words of Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman, authors of </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/15eb45f0-3c51-42e3-8319-8e88d9b0c8b3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Underground Empire: How America Weaponized the World Economy</span></a></em><span>, the dollar’s role gives the U.S. government a “panopticon” — it can see everything — and a “chokepoint” — it can cut nations off from the world economy, a power it demonstrated most notably by imposing sanctions on Iran over the years. These sanctions played a key role in getting Iran to sign President Obama’s 2015 </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f9ab5010-d043-4f7b-9f60-427bbf887daa?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action</span></a><span>, in which Iran agreed to limit its nuclear program in return for a relaxation of sanctions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Donald Trump ripped up the JCPOA, which he</span><span> derided as</span><span> a terrible deal. </span><span>Now the Iranian regime is in a much stronger position than it was under the JCPOA. Yet we should also recognize that while the U.S. has suffered a military failure, it has also suffered a financial power failure. China has </span><span>used the war to strengthen an alternative </span><span>global </span><span>payments system that bypasses the dollar — and hence allows governments that are at odds with America to evade both U.S. surveillance and U.S. sanctions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7b0056af-e2a3-487c-aa6a-57d66732d8f6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Wall Street Journal</a><span> recently explained, Iran was able to continue selling oil (until the U.S. temporarily imposed a military blockade) and buying essential imports, despite U.S. financial sanctions, by taking payment in yuan and using those yuan to buy Chinese goods. Ships that paid Iran for safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz also paid in yuan (or in cryptocurrency, whose only real use case remains criminal activity.) The details are complicated, but using yuan essentially allows those</span><span> designated by</span><span> the U.S. government </span><span>as </span><span>rogue actors to fly under our financial radar.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s true that Iran and Russia had significantly increased their yuan-based transactions before the war began. </span><span>But the war offered an object lesson in the usefulness of the yuan as an alternative currency. Other nations, including the United Arab Emirates, are now considering accepting payment in yuan. And the war has also given a boost to China’s Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS), an alternative to SWIFT, the Belgium-based but effectively U.S.-controlled system that still settles the great bulk of international transactions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I don’t want to overstate the case here. The dollar’s role as the dominant currency for ordinary business is not under threat. A new article in Foreign Policy by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0abcfcdb-4897-44e1-bb87-1779cfda860d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Agathe Demarais</a><span> is titled “China’s de-dollarization drive has hit a wall.” It points out that overall use both of CIPS and of yuan remain quite modest compared with the SWIFT/dollar system. Doing business in dollars remains easier and cheaper than using any other currency, and will remain so unless U.S. policy becomes even more self-destructive.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Yet something important has happened. The Iran debacle has demonstrated that using dollars and retaining access to the U.S. banking system, while convenient, aren’t necessary.</span><span> Iran’s ability to withstand American pressure has demonstrated that U.S. sanctions are a lot less effective than in the past given that rogue actors can use the yuan and CIPS as a work-around. And as the Gulf States’ actions show, even countries that are U.S. allies are now considering signing onto the Chinese payment system.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As I wrote a few weeks ago, recent events — not just the failed war on Iran but the limited effects of Trump’s tariffs and, in a different way, Ukraine’s survival without U.S. aid — have shown that America is now an </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/20689ef4-bbf5-47e6-82d6-24684581e22c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">inessential nation</a><span>. Trump thought that throwing America’s weight around would show the world how powerful he is. Instead, he </span><span>made us weaker and the world knows it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>MUSICAL CODA</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Working for the Yankee dollar? Not so much, now.</span></p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/6f3142b0-b383-43c6-bd76-1a6cc4529ebb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="margin-bottom: 0;display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/WiayZdPESno" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. on the Dutch center-left about the problems of the world. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At one point the group was meeting with one of the junior PvdA ministers in the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/63c5838d-97b0-4d2f-ba89-6ee418876ca6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">fourth Balkenende cabinet</a><span>, and he said that immigration is a more challenging issue for European social democrats than for Americans. His explanation was that America has a streak of explicit propositional nationalism to it — Superman can talk about “truth, justice, and the American Way,” but there’s no Dutch Way. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I was genuinely taken aback by this and said to him of course there’s a Dutch Way. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>He didn’t know what I was talking about, so I told him that I was taught in school very specifically that New York City’s traditions of tolerance and diversity are Dutch values that were passed down to us by the settlers of New Amsterdam. We’re not, like, running around speaking Dutch in New York and certainly not promoting an ethnic state of Dutch-ancestry people. But we celebrate our understanding of Dutch culture and Dutch values, and if we can tell wave after wave of immigrants to New York that they are welcome in the city for Dutch reasons but also must learn to practice open-mindedness and tolerance for Dutch reasons, then surely they can do it in the Netherlands!</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">¹</span><span> </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This guy probably thought I was putting him on. Dutch values in New York? So I started talking like crazy conspiracy guy about how the Mets wear orange and blue because the Dodgers wore blue and the Giants wore orange, and orange and blue are the colors of the flag of New York City because those are the colors of the Netherlands. The Knicks, too, wear orange and blue. And of course, Knicks stands for Knickerbockers, which is some kind of long-obsolete ethnic term for people of Dutch ancestry. </p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size:
